textTitles: Staff handbook — working away from the office

texts.label: A
texts.title: Staff handbook — working away from the office

paragraphs.text: Staff handbook, section 9: working away from the office. Employees who have completed six months of service may apply to work from home for up to three days a week. Applications are made through the staff portal and are answered by your line manager within ten working days. A refusal must give a business reason in writing, and you may ask for the decision to be reviewed once by the department head. An arrangement that has been agreed is reviewed after six months, and either side may end it with four weeks’ notice.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Whatever is agreed, the company remains responsible for your health and safety while you are working. Before a home-working arrangement begins you must complete the online workstation assessment, which takes about twenty minutes and asks about your chair, screen height, lighting and the space you have available. Where the assessment identifies a problem, the company will supply a chair, a monitor stand or a desk lamp; it does not pay for desks, broadband or heating. Equipment supplied remains company property and must be returned when the arrangement ends or you leave.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Home workers keep the same core hours as the office, 10 am to 4 pm, and are expected to be reachable in that window by telephone and in the company chat. Outside those hours you may organise your day as you wish, provided the agreed work is done. Meetings that include even one person working from home should be held online rather than in a room, so that nobody joins at a disadvantage; the exception is the quarterly planning day, which everybody attends in person and for which travel is paid.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Documents marked confidential may be opened at home but may not be printed there, and paper brought home must be returned to the office for shredding. If you intend to work from a country other than the one in which you are employed, you must have written approval in advance, because tax and insurance rules differ; approval for such work is granted for a maximum of twenty working days in any calendar year. Line managers may refuse a request for home working during a probation period or while a formal performance review is open.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The Fenwick Engineering apprenticeship: how the first year works. Apprentices join in September on a two-year contract and are paid from the first day. The year is divided between four days a week on site and one day a week at the technical college, and the college day is timetabled for Wednesdays. Attendance at college is part of the contract: a missed college day counts in the same way as a missed day at work and must be explained to your supervisor.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: On site, apprentices move between three departments — assembly, quality and maintenance — spending roughly four months in each. The order differs from apprentice to apprentice and depends on where a place is free, so do not expect to follow the same route as a colleague. Each department has a named mentor who keeps a record of the tasks you have completed. That record, not the college marks, decides whether you move to the second year, and it is discussed with you at the end of every placement.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Tools and protective clothing are issued in the first week. Boots and overalls are yours to keep; measuring instruments are signed out and must be returned at the end of each placement in working order. Damage that happens during normal work is not charged to the apprentice, but instruments lost through carelessness are replaced at cost. Safety training is repeated every six months regardless of experience, and an apprentice who misses a safety session may not work on the shop floor until it has been made up.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Pay rises at the start of the second year and again on completion. Holiday is twenty-five days plus public holidays, and apprentices are asked not to take holiday during college terms. Those who complete the programme are guaranteed an interview for any vacancy at the company for which they are qualified, though not a job; in recent years about seven in ten have been taken on directly. The remainder leave with a recognised qualification, a record of completed work and a reference from their last mentor.
paragraphs.label: D
